summary: Defines the application/whoispp-response media type. Together with RFC 2957, it lets MIME-aware mail software and other systems carry Whois++ transactions.

eli5.summary: Whois++ is a lookup service. This gives its answers a label so email can carry them back.

questions: how are whois++ answers sent in mime
what is a whois++ server-to-ask record
subtitle: Registers a MIME type that carries Whois++ server answers, the other half of a Whois++ transaction in mail.

tldr.problem: Whois++ answers had no standard way to travel inside MIME-aware mail software and other systems that use Internet media types.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers the media type application/whoispp-response and gives an ABNF grammar for a subset of the responses a Whois++ server sends back to a valid query.
tldr.outcome: Together with RFC 2957, which covers the queries, MIME software can carry complete Whois++ transactions. The type has no native authentication.

today: RFC 2958 is an Informational memo and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion for queries is RFC 2957.

sections.title: What the Type Is For
sections.content: RFC 2958 defines how responses of the Whois++ protocol (RFC 1835) are expressed as a MIME media type (RFC 2046). Together with RFC 2957, which defines the query type, it is meant to let MIME-enabled mail software and other systems that use Internet media types carry out Whois++ transactions.
sections.eli5: The questions have their own label in the sister memo. This memo labels the answers that come back.

sections.title: The MIME Registration
sections.content: Section 1 is a registration template addressed to IANA. The type name is application and the subtype is whoispp-response. There are no required or optional parameters, any valid MIME encodings may be used, the published specification is the RFC itself, and the intended usage is common.
sections.eli5: This is the form that gets the new label added to the official list of labels.

sections.title: Response Structure
sections.content:
The grammar uses the ABNF-like notation of RFC 2234 and defines a subset of the responses expected from a Whois++ server after a valid query. A server response is either a good message, then the output, then an end message, or a bad message followed by an end message. Lines end with CR LF.

The output is one of four forms, matching the query's format constraint: full, abridged, summary or handle. Full, abridged and handle output can also include server-to-ask records that refer the client to another server.

Each record is a block that starts with a marker line and ends with an END line. The markers are the words FULL, ABRIDGED, SUMMARY, HANDLE and SERVER-TO-ASK, each written after a hash sign. Full records hold attribute name and value lines; a summary record reports Matches, an optional Referrals count and the templates; a server-to-ask record gives the server handle, host name, host port and optionally a protocol.
sections.eli5: An answer is a stack of cards. Each card starts with a title line, lists its facts, and ends with a line saying END.

sections.title: Status Messages
sections.content:
Response lines that start with % and a three-digit number carry status messages, which may be several lines long. A good response begins with a % 200 message, while a bad response begins with a message starting % 5 followed by two digits. The grammar also lists % 226 and % 203 as start markers for the closing messages.

The syntax allows such messages to appear between records, so a client can separate data lines from status lines by the leading %.
sections.eli5: Lines beginning with a percent sign are notes from the server, like "all good" at the start or a goodbye at the end.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The type carries purely descriptive information with no directives. The RFC notes concerns about the appropriateness (privacy) of the information provided and about its authenticity, and says the content type provides no native mechanisms for authentication.
sections.eli5: The label does not prove an answer is true or that it is safe to share, so those checks have to happen elsewhere.

data.title: Response grammar (excerpt)
data.code:
server          =   goodmessage mnl output mnl endmessage nl
                    / badmessage nl endmessage nl

output          =   full / abridged / summary / handle

full-record     =   "# FULL " template serverhandle localhandle
                           system-nl
                    1*(fulldata system-nl)
                    "# END" system-nl

summary-record  =  "# SUMMARY " serverhandle system-nl
                    summarydata
                    "# END" system-nl
